findings.paper_title: PIs Monitoring and TM strategy Q1 2026/27 - Main Report
findings.headline: The council is planning to draw down useable reserves over the MTFS period to support the revenue budget
findings.detail: The Liability Benchmark revision explicitly includes 'the increased draw down of useable reserves anticipated to support the revenue budget over the MTFS period.' This indicates the council cannot balance current revenue spending from income and is relying on reserve depletion.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown to fund revenue is a sign of structural deficit; finite reserves depleting annually will eventually create a financial cliff unless underlying spending or income patterns change, creating risk for creditors.
findings.figures: Drawdown amount not quantified in this report
findings.quote: The inputs that determine the Liability Benchmark have been revised to include the increased capital expenditure relating to vehicle leasing and the increased draw down of useable reserves anticipated to support the revenue budget over the MTFS period.

findings.paper_title: PIs Monitoring and TM strategy Q1 2026/27 - Main Report
findings.headline: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream increased to 13.20% from the approved 9.30%, a 42% increase
findings.detail: The share of revenue budget consumed by financing costs has risen sharply from budget: 9.30% approved to 13.20% actual at Q1. This indicates either lower-than-expected revenue or higher-than-expected financing demands. The paper's treasury section does not explicitly explain the increase.
findings.matters: A rising financing ratio reduces budgetary flexibility for service delivery and indicates tightening affordability; it is a key metric for lenders assessing whether the council can service debt while maintaining service levels.
findings.figures: Approved 9.30%, Q1 actual 13.20%; increase of 3.9 percentage points
findings.quote: Estimated Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream 9.30% 13.20%

findings.paper_title: PIs Monitoring and TM strategy Q1 2026/27 - Main Report
findings.headline: Capital expenditure forecast has fallen to £18.823m from £44.265m budgeted in February—a 57% reduction in the first quarter
findings.detail: The council's capital expenditure forecast for 2026/27 has been substantially revised downward from the February budget. The council attributes this to 'additional slippage in the capital programme.' This reduction of £25.4m represents a major change in planned capital investment within the first quarter of the financial year.
findings.matters: Significant capital slippage can signal project delivery challenges, procurement delays, or inability to execute planned investment; it affects the CFR and medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Budgeted £44.265m (February 2026), forecast £18.823m (30 June 2026)—a reduction of £25.442m
findings.quote: The current figure takes account of additional slippage in the capital programme where spend will now be incurred in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Monitoring 2026/27 Q1 - Main Report
findings.headline: Pride in Place grant of £1.5m must be fully spent by 31 March 2027, requiring acceleration or risk of clawback
findings.detail: The council received £1.5m in Pride in Place Impact Fund grant which must be spent by 31 March 2027. The council is already managing slippage by stating that "funding may be allocated to alternative schemes if any approved scheme is not likely to complete by the deadline". Additionally, £230k of a separate £270k parks grant will be shifted to 2027/28.
findings.matters: Time-bound grant funding creates a hard deadline for expenditure and introduces execution risk. Failure to spend triggers grant clawback, which would require either reserve funding or project cancellation.
findings.figures: £1.5m grant; £230k of £270k additional parks grant shifted to 2027/28; deadline 31 March 2027
findings.quote: The Council has received grant funding of £1.5m which must be spent by 31 st March 2027. This funding has been allocated to several schemes which will be closely monitored to ensure completion by the deadline. Funding may be allocated to alternative schemes if any approved scheme is not likely to complete by the deadline.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Monitoring 2026/27 Q1 - Main Report
findings.headline: Only 18% of rephased capital budget spent by Q1 despite £25.923m of projects rephased into future years
findings.detail: As of 30 June 2026, the council had spent or committed only £3.412m of the rephased £18.824m budget for 2026/27, representing 18.12% of planned spend. Meanwhile, £25.923m (58% of the approved capital budget) has been rephased into 2027/28. This combination suggests either slow project starts or significant delivery slippage beyond what has yet been formally recognized.
findings.matters: Consistently low Q1 spend relative to rephased budgets indicates either optimistic forecasting or execution constraints that will compound cash flow and borrowing requirements in future years.
findings.figures: £3.412m spent/committed of £18.824m budget at Q1; £25.923m rephased to 2027/28; 18.12% spend rate
findings.quote: As of 30th June 2026, actual and committed expenditure totals £3.412m, representing 18.12% of the rephased 2026/27 budget of £18.824m.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Monitoring 2026/27 Q1 - Main Report
findings.headline: Capital programme complexity and scale placing significant demands on staffing and delivery capacity
findings.detail: The capital programme has grown substantially to £44.747m. The report notes that "the increased scale and complexity of the programme are placing significant demands on the Council's staffing and delivery capacity". The council acknowledges that "it is essential that all projects are strategically planned, adequately resourced, and appropriately phased" and warns the programme "may require further revisions in its phasing in the future".
findings.matters: A council acknowledging that its capital programme is outpacing its delivery capacity signals risk of further slippage, cost overruns, or poor project management. This affects programme credibility and borrowing sustainability.
findings.figures: £44.747m total capital programme; 89% funded through external grants and contributions
findings.quote: The Capital Programme has grown substantially over the past two financial years and now totals £44.747m. While approximately 89% of this funding is secured through external grants and contributions, the increased scale and complexity of the programme are placing significant demands on the Council's staffing and delivery capacity.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Monitoring 2026/27 Q1 - Main Report
findings.headline: Market Chambers match funding of £2m slipped pending Heritage Lottery bid decision in March 2027, creating delivery uncertainty
findings.detail: The council committed £2m as match funding for Market Chambers (part of the Levelling Up market regeneration scheme). This has been rephased out of 2026/27 because the Heritage Lottery bid for the delivery stage is now scheduled for November 2026 with decision expected March 2027. This makes Q4 2027 the earliest realistic start for this element of work.
findings.matters: Project delivery is contingent on a third-party grant decision with no certainty until March 2027. This reduces the council's control over its capital spend profile and could affect overall programme completion.
findings.figures: £2m match funding slipped; Heritage Lottery bid November 2026; decision expected March 2027
findings.quote: A further £2m of estimated slippage relates to the match funding required at Market Chambers. The Heritage Lottery bid for the delivery stage is now scheduled for November 2026 with a decision expected around March 2027

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Monitoring 2026/27 Q1 - Main Report
findings.headline: Huncoat Garden Village timing rephased by £22.762m following revised Homes England grant agreement, shifting 86% of budgeted spend into 2027/28
findings.detail: Huncoat Garden Village was budgeted at £26.262m for 2026/27 but the council has now rephased £22.762m into 2027/28 "in line with the revised grant funding agreement with Homes England". Current activity remains in preparatory stages—planning, legal, land acquisition, and CPO documentation. The project is fully funded by a £29.897m Homes England grant, of which £3.0m has been received to date.
findings.matters: This is the largest single project in the capital programme and is entirely dependent on Homes England's grant draw schedule and CPO outcome. Delay in planning or legal process would force further slippage and could affect council cash flow and delivery credibility.
findings.figures: £26.262m total budget; £22.762m rephased to 2027/28; £3.0m of £29.897m grant received
findings.quote: Huncoat Garden Village remains a major strategic scheme for the Council, fully funded by a £29.897m grant from Homes England. Forecast expenditure is phased over three financial years, with £0.710m spent in 2025/26, £26.262m budgeted spend in 2026/27, and the balance in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Monitoring 2026/27 Q1 - Main Report
findings.headline: Capital receipts shortfall creates funding gap of £1.906m against a programme dependent on asset sales
findings.detail: The council's capital programme requires £4.894m in capital receipts from asset disposal. As of Q1, only £2.988m has been generated, leaving £1.906m still to be achieved. The report explicitly flags this as a high-level risk. The council states it will "continue to review the Council's operational asset base to identify further disposal opportunities" but provides no timeline or confidence level for closing this gap.
findings.matters: A shortfall in capital receipts would force the council to either defer projects, increase borrowing, or draw reserves to fund its capital programme. This is a live funding risk, not a planning issue.
findings.figures: £4.894m required; £2.988m generated to date; £1.906m shortfall
findings.quote: The Financing of the capital programme is dependent on securing £4.894m in capital receipts from the sale of Council-owned land and buildings. To date £2.988m has been generated, leaving a balance of £1.906m to be achieved.

findings.paper_title: Hyndburn Leisure - Provisional Revenue Outturn 2025/2026 - Main Report
findings.headline: Council's four-year subsidy reduction plan, from £1m to £350k, is at risk after trust failed to land savings in year one despite full subsidy payment
findings.detail: The council agreed in March 2026 to reduce subsidy from £1m (actual 2024/25) to £700k (2025/26) to £500k (2026/27) to £350k (2027/28), underpinned by Hyndburn Leisure delivering cost reductions. In the first year of reduced subsidy, the trust has overshooted budget by £34.7k and failed to meet its own savings targets. This suggests the annual 20-25% subsidy reductions are not achievable.
findings.matters: The entire partnership restructuring following the write-off of £1.624m historic debt is premised on rapid subsidy reduction. If the trust cannot reduce costs even in year one, the sustainability of the partnership and the council's financial forecasts are both at risk.
findings.quote: Rather than making a physical payment to Hyndburn Leisure for £700,000, the subsidy amount has been offset against the outstanding trading debt due to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Hyndburn Leisure - Provisional Revenue Outturn 2025/2026 - Main Report
findings.headline: Cath Thom Leisure Centre, opened October 2025, showed a £117.5k operating loss in its first six months of partial-year operation
findings.detail: The new facility opened in October 2025, so 2025/26 outturn reflects only six months. Despite this, the centre showed a significant loss attributed to higher operating costs including utilities. Forecast for 2026/27 is a £61.2k surplus, representing a dramatic turnaround from loss to profit once in full-year operation, but this depends on cost assumptions proving correct.
findings.matters: Major new capital investments should demonstrate quick path to profitability. A loss of £117.5k in six months is material and suggests either the facility design was uneconomic or cost assumptions for full-year operation are at risk.
findings.figures: £117.5k loss 2025/26 (part-year); £61.2k forecast surplus 2026/27 (full-year); facility opened October 2025
findings.quote: The facility only opened in October 2025, meaning the draft 2025/26 position reflects a part-year of operation, including the early mobilisation and establishment phase. It is expected that there will be a movement from the provisional outturn deficit of £117.5k in 2025/26 to a forecast surplus of £61.2k in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Hyndburn Leisure - Provisional Revenue Outturn 2025/2026 - Main Report
findings.headline: Electricity costs overran by £82k, reaching £551.9k, with material contribution from higher than budgeted costs at newly opened Cath Thom centre
findings.detail: Premises costs overran budget by £104.8k, primarily driven by electricity that exceeded budget by £82k. Performance was better than budget in the first half of the year but deteriorated significantly in the second half, particularly due to higher than estimated energy costs at Cath Thom Leisure Centre which opened in October 2025. This represents a structural cost pressure.
findings.matters: Utilities are a material cost that the trust is struggling to control, particularly for new facilities. This suggests energy cost assumptions in the subsidy reduction plan may be optimistic, and cost pressures may persist.
findings.figures: £551.9k electricity costs; £82k overspend vs budget; £104.8k total premises overspend
findings.quote: Electricity costs totalled £551.9k at the end of the year. This was a notable movement from the position earlier in the year, when electricity was performing better than budget during the first half of the financial year. Higher than estimated energy costs at The Cath Thom Leisure Centre played a significant role in the final electricity overspend, contributing to the adverse year-end position.

findings.paper_title: Hyndburn Leisure - Provisional Revenue Outturn 2025/2026 - Main Report
findings.headline: Hyndburn Leisure overshot budget by £34.7k in 2025/26 after failing to achieve required savings of £58.4k
findings.detail: The trust set a £58.4k savings target to bring the operating deficit down to enable the £700k council subsidy to break even. These savings were not achieved, leaving an operating loss of £54.8k against a budgeted loss of £43.7k. The trust did not request additional subsidy but is forecasting to cover this 2025/26 deficit through 2026/27 trading, requiring new savings plans.
findings.matters: The council is implementing a four-year subsidy reduction plan from £1m to £350k, contingent on the trust reducing costs. Failure to land savings in year one of this plan raises questions about whether the trajectory is achievable.
findings.figures: £58,417 savings target not achieved; £34,689 provisional overspend; £43,741 budgeted loss vs £54,791 actual loss
findings.quote: The impact of higher utility costs at the Cath Thom Leisure centre has resulted in these savings not being achieved and the trust will need to find additional savings in 2026/2027 to cover the 2025/2026 loss of 34.7k.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/27 Q1 - Main Report
findings.headline: Staffing pressures of £499k across multiple services indicate budget gaps
findings.detail: The council forecast £499k staffing pressures against the original budget, spread across services. Key examples include Legal and Land Charges (agency worker cover £46k), Environmental Health (specialist advice £43k), Planning (£24k), HR (£24k), and Property (£120k staffing costs). These are forecast variances, not new recruitment.
findings.matters: Persistent staffing pressures across departments suggest the original budget does not capture true staffing costs. This indicates either recruitment/retention difficulties driving higher costs, or chronic budget gaps the council cannot address.
findings.figures: Total staffing pressures: £499k; agency worker (Legal): £46k; specialist advice (Environmental Health): £43k; Planning: £24k; HR: £24k; Property staffing: £120k
findings.quote: Staffing Pressures - £499

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/27 Q1 - Main Report
findings.headline: Unrecoverable housing benefit payments of £203k creating service overspend
findings.detail: Revenue, Benefits and Customer Contact service is forecasting £237k overspend. While staffing costs provide (£76k) underspend, this is offset by IT system costs (£90k), legal fees (£15k), and crucially, unrecoverable housing benefit payments of £203k. The paper does not explain the cause of these unrecoverable payments.
findings.matters: Unrecoverable benefit payments signal either deprivation/demand pressures in the population served, or administration/collection weakness in the benefits service. Both are material to a lender assessing council health.
findings.figures: £203k unrecoverable HB payments; total service overspend £237k
findings.quote: whilst there are staffing underspends of (£76k), these are off-set by pressures in IT system costs £90k, legal fees £15k and unrecoverable housing benefit payments £203k

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/27 Q1 - Main Report
findings.headline: Forecast drawdown of reserves from £25.1m to £11.0m through use for capital financing
findings.detail: Opening reserve balances stand at £25.091m (closed 2025/26). The council forecasts a total call on reserves of £14.049m in 2026/27, including £12.437m for capital financing, leaving closing balances of £11.042m. This represents a 56% reduction in reserves in a single year.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion to this degree materially reduces the council's financial flexibility for future years. A lender would need to understand whether the capital financing pattern is sustainable and what headroom remains for unexpected demands.
findings.figures: Opening: £25.091m; Forecast closing: £11.042m; Total call on reserves: £14.049m (including £12.437m for capital financing)
findings.quote: At the present time the forecast call on reserves stands at £14.049m, including reserves to be used to fund capital financing.

findings.paper_title: Annual Audit Report 2025-26 APP
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will eliminate this council in April 2028 with no clear plan for staff retention
findings.detail: Hyndburn will be absorbed into a unitary authority on 1 April 2028. The audit report flags that staff departures through early retirement are likely and that 2027/28 audit work will need to shift emphasis to complete pending items before the council ceases to exist. Risk management processes are being adjusted for this transition but institutional knowledge loss is an acknowledged threat.
findings.matters: Structural dissolution creates acute operational risk in the final two years; potential loss of experienced finance and control staff before systems and processes are properly transferred could leave controls weakened during a critical wind-down period.
findings.figures: Vesting date 1 April 2028; reorganisation decision pending Secretary of State approval
findings.quote: 2027/28 will be the last year of the existence of Hyndburn Borough Council and as a result this will have to be reflected in the 2027/28 Internal Audit Plan with a change in emphasis for some areas of work to try and ensure that as far as possible everything is at a completed state prior to the vesting date of the newly formed Unitary Council on 1st April 2028. The Audit Team will assist Service Areas across the Council in addressing any risks that may arise, for example because of loss of staff, some of whom may choose to retire prior to the start of the replacement Unitary Authority.

findings.paper_title: Annual Audit Report 2025-26 APP
findings.headline: Payroll system migration created control weaknesses and payment errors that remain only partially remediated
findings.detail: The council's migration to new payroll software resulted in the only Limited Assurance audit opinion of the year. Issues included the system's inability to handle car allowances over 70 miles correctly, confusion over sick pay setup for multi-post contracts, and software errors causing pay errors that required manual workarounds. Follow-up work found 4 of 9 agreed actions fully implemented and 5 only partially implemented.
findings.matters: Payroll errors and incomplete remediation indicate unresolved control weaknesses in a critical financial system; slow action completion suggests either system limitations the council cannot overcome or lack of management capacity to resolve.
findings.figures: One Limited Assurance opinion; 9 recommendations issued; 4 fully implemented, 5 partially implemented at follow-up
findings.quote: The Council had migrated to a new Payroll software system, and the issues were a mixture of the software not being able to correctly deal with a small number of issues, the software not being able to distinguish car allowance journeys over 70 miles where different rules applied... There was some examples of software errors that had resulted in pay errors that in turn created work that included manual calculations.

findings.paper_title: PIs Monitoring and TM Strategy Update - Q4 2025/26 - Main Report
findings.headline: Council enhancing counterparty due diligence for £24m in loans to other local authorities amid sector financial stress
findings.detail: In response to the increasing number of Section 114 Notices being issued across local government, the council is undertaking additional due diligence before approving new loans to other councils. Checks include reviewing local press for financial distress, analysing latest financial statements, and assessing overall financial health. The council currently holds £24m in loans outstanding to 12 other local authorities.
findings.matters: Demonstrates prudent risk management and awareness of sector-wide distress, but also exposes the council's concentration risk with £24m lent to other councils that may themselves be in financial difficulty
findings.figures: £24m lent to 12 local authorities at rates ranging from 4.15% to 4.75%
findings.quote: To ensure the Council is considering any possible risk posed by the recent increase in Section 114 Notices being issued, we are undertaking additional due diligence, which includes: Reviewing local press for any signs of financial distress.

findings.paper_title: PIs Monitoring and TM Strategy Update - Q4 2025/26 - Main Report
findings.headline: Investment income exceeded budget by £900k due to higher-than-anticipated interest rates and above-forecast cash balances
findings.detail: Interest receivable on temporary lending was £1.6m against a budget of £700k, a £900k favourable variance. This outperformance resulted from the council holding higher cash balances than forecast (due to advance grants and capital slippage) combined with interest rates remaining elevated above budget assumptions.
findings.matters: While positive in headline terms, the outperformance masks the underlying fact of £28.7m held in temporary investments, suggesting significant cash tied up that may indicate capital deployment difficulties
findings.figures: Budget £700k, actual £1.6m (£900k variance); total short-term investments £28.726m
findings.quote: The actual income from investment interest for the year ending 31 March 2026 is £1.6m; an increase of £900k against the original budget forecast.

findings.paper_title: PIs Monitoring and TM Strategy Update - Q4 2025/26 - Main Report
findings.headline: Finance lease interest costs overran budget by £175k due to shift in vehicle procurement strategy
findings.detail: Interest payable on finance leases was £216k against a budget of £41k (£175k overspend). This reflects a procurement strategy change where vehicles previously purchased are now being leased, including four additional refuse collection vehicles for food waste. Minimum revenue provision charges are also higher than budgeted due to this leasing approach.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted revenue pressure indicates divergence between budget assumptions and actual procurement decisions, requiring reforecasting and potentially signalling financial pressures driving shift to leasing
findings.figures: Finance lease interest budget £41k, actual £216k (£175k overspend); 4 additional RCVs leased
findings.quote: An estimate of interest on additional borrowing was included in the budget and whilst there were no new borrowing requirements for capital spend, the changes required for lease accounting and the timing of the leases being taken resulted in a pressure against the 2025/26 revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: PIs Monitoring and TM Strategy Update - Q4 2025/26 - Main Report
findings.headline: Capital expenditure underspent by £6.15m (23%) with slippage carried into 2026/27
findings.detail: Approved capital expenditure of £26.054m achieved only £19.904m in actual spend. This reflects additional slippage carried forward from prior year and further slippage within the current year. The council attributes this to difficulty deploying advance grants and capital programme execution challenges.
findings.matters: Persistent capital slippage indicates planning and execution challenges, delays asset acquisition timelines, and leaves advance funding undeployed
findings.figures: Approved £26.054m, actual £19.904m, variance £6.15m (23%)
findings.quote: Investment balances were higher than had been forecast when the Prudential Indicators and strategy were set. This is mainly due to grants received in advance of capital spend being incurred, as well as slippage in the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn 2025/26 - Main Report
findings.headline: Accrington Town Centre Development pressure of £204k while Market Hall, Market Chambers and Burton Chambers remained not operational
findings.detail: The council incurred £204k of additional costs to maintain Accrington Town Centre facilities while key civic venues were not operational, offsetting £63k of staffing underspends. The document does not explain why the venues were closed, the expected reopening date, or whether this reflects renovation delays or unplanned operational issues.
findings.matters: Non-operational venues in a town-centre regeneration project raise questions about project progress and cost control. This indicates the council's major economic development initiative is experiencing complications, with ongoing holding costs and uncertain timelines affecting budget outcomes.
findings.figures: £204k net pressure; £63k staffing underspend absorbed by closure costs
findings.quote: Whilst underspends have occurred in relation to staffing (£63k), additional costs have been incurred whilst the Market Hall, Market Chambers and Burton chambers were not operational. This has resulted in an overall pressure of £204k.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn 2025/26 - Main Report
findings.headline: Capital programme delivered £8.244m less than planned; £8.244m additional reserves retained due to capital slippage into 2026/27
findings.detail: Expected reserves were forecast to fall to £16.849m but ended at £25.093m, primarily because capital expenditure was deferred. Significant projects delayed include Huncoat Garden Village (£2.9m), leisure works, levelling-up schemes (£7m), food waste schemes, and disabled facilities grants (£1.569m). This pattern suggests either delivery challenges or sequencing issues in the capital programme.
findings.matters: Consistent deferral of capital spending indicates execution risk or project delays. For a council dependent on government capital grants (which now amount to £4.762m unspent), inability to deploy grants on schedule may risk future funding eligibility and signals weaknesses in infrastructure delivery capability.
findings.figures: £8.244m reserves increase due to capital slippage; £4.762m capital grants carried forward unspent; £14.481m capital grants deployed in year
findings.quote: The provisional closing balance is £25.093m, an (£8.244m) increase to the January estimate. This is due to a number of factors such as additional grants and capital receipts being received, capital expenditure being slipped into 2026/27 and additional underspends being transferred to reserves for future use.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn 2025/26 - Main Report
findings.headline: Treasury investment income of £901k driving the headline underspend is one-off and will not repeat
findings.detail: Additional investment income of £901k resulted from higher interest rates and significant cash balances available to invest. This income is entirely dependent on interest rate conditions that will normalise, making it a non-recurring benefit. When stripped out, the underlying operational position is significantly tighter than the headline £1.337m underspend suggests.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors need to understand the structural financial position, not headline numbers inflated by temporary interest rate conditions. This one-off gain masks whether the council is operationally balanced or running a deficit funded by asset returns that will disappear.
findings.figures: £901k additional investment income from interest rates; offset by £147k leasing interest
findings.quote: Additional treasury investment income of (£901k) has been achieved due to the increase in interest rates and the significant balances that the Council has been able to invest, largely due to the upfront receipt of capital grants, however this has been offset by leasing interest of £147k.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn 2025/26 - Main Report
findings.headline: Benefits and Customer Contact overspent by £845k, principally from non-recoverable Housing Benefit claims
findings.detail: The service overspent by £845k due to non-recoverable benefit claims, legal fees, downward correction of government grant forecasts, and IT maintenance. The council states that the majority of these impacts were one-off or have been reduced in future budgets, suggesting control or eligibility verification issues that required remediation.
findings.matters: Non-recoverable Housing Benefit payments at this scale (£845k) indicate either control weaknesses in eligibility checking or unexpected circumstances that overwhelmed safeguards. This matters to lenders assessing the council's financial management capability and to finance directors monitoring compliance risk.
findings.figures: £845k overspend; stated as majority one-off or reduced going forward
findings.quote: The service has overspent by £845k, which is due primarily to non-recoverable Housing Benefit claims, legal fees, the correction of forecasts for government grant income, which is no longer receivable and additional spend on IT maintenance. The majority of impacts were either one-off or have been reduced in future budgets.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Outturn 2025/26 - Main Report
findings.headline: Capital financed 73% from external grants and 26% from earmarked reserves, consuming significant reserve capacity in a single year
findings.detail: The £19.904m outturn was financed by £14.481m external grants, £5.223m from earmarked reserves, £0.103m capital receipts, and £0.030m revenue. The council used zero prudential borrowing despite needing to draw heavily on reserves and external funding to deliver the programme.
findings.matters: High grant dependency (73%) creates risk if external funding is withdrawn or conditions breached; using 26% of capital financing from earmarked reserves in a single year could constrain financial flexibility and the council's capacity to respond to emergencies
findings.figures: External grants £14,480,923 (73%), Earmarked reserves £5,223,208 (26%), Capital receipts £102,687 (1%), Prudential borrowing £0
findings.quote: The £19.904m outturn has largely been financed using external grant monies received and the use of capital receipts and reserves held by the council. There has been no use of prudential borrowing in the financing of the programme

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Outturn 2025/26 - Main Report
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage totals £36.230m (64% of the £56.148m approved programme), concentrated on major transformation schemes
findings.detail: Beyond Huncoat's £26.076m, the Levelling Up-funded Accrington Town Centre scheme accounts for £6.454m slippage and Oswaldtwistle Civic Theatre for £0.515m. The pattern of delays across multiple larger initiatives suggests either delivery capacity constraints or issues with external-funded schemes meeting their timetables.
findings.matters: Systemic slippage across the council's largest projects signals potential execution risks and raises questions about original planning and delivery capability, both material to lenders evaluating the council's financial and operational credibility
findings.figures: £36.230m total slippage from £56.148m programme (64%); Huncoat £26.076m, Levelling Up £6.454m, Civic Theatre £0.515m
findings.quote: £36.230m of budget has been rephrased into 2026/2027. £26.076m relates to the scheme at Huncoat Garden Village, £6.454m relates to the Levelling Up scheme for Accrington Town Centre, £0.515m to Oswaldtwistle Civic Theatre Refurbishment Works

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Outturn 2025/26 - Main Report
findings.headline: Huncoat Garden Village project delivered only £2.925m of its £29.187m revised budget, with £26.076m slipped to 2026/27
findings.detail: The council budgeted £29.187m for Huncoat Garden Village in 2025/26 but spent only £2.925m, with £26.262m rephrased into 2026/27 and beyond. This 89% slippage on what was the largest single project represents a material delivery shortfall and suggests either execution challenges or external constraints preventing progress.
findings.matters: Large project delays of this magnitude raise questions about the council's capacity to execute transformational schemes, a key factor lenders consider when assessing financial resilience and investment credibility
findings.figures: £29.187m revised programme, £2.925m actual spend, £26.262m slipped to 2026/27
findings.quote: £36.230m of budget has been rephrased into 2026/2027. £26.076m relates to the scheme at Huncoat Garden Village

findings.paper_title: b) Capital Programme 2026/27 - 2028/29
findings.headline: Programme risk is explicitly acknowledged as elevated compared to previous years, despite mitigation steps
findings.detail: The Council states directly that 'the level of risk remains increased compared to previous years due to the size of the overall programme' (total £38.6m including slippage). To mitigate, the Council has appointed professional project managers and cost control experts for the two largest projects. The acknowledgement of elevated risk persisting despite these steps indicates material delivery challenge.
findings.matters: Larger programmes carry higher exposure to cost overruns, delivery delays and budget pressure; elevated risk persisting after mitigation suggests structural challenges
findings.figures: Total programme £38.565m (including £30.706m slippage); £22.366m Huncoat Garden Village; £6.251m Levelling Up
findings.quote: The programme contains a limited amount of risk this year. The level of risk remains increased compared to previous years due to the size of the overall programme. However, to further reduce the risk the Council has supplemented its own project management and cost control capacity by the appointment of experienced professionals in both disciplines for its two largest projects.

findings.paper_title: b) Capital Programme 2026/27 - 2028/29
findings.headline: Capital reserves are being materially committed: £3m drawn for 2026/27 additions plus £2m earmarked for future Heritage works
findings.detail: The Council's 2026/27 capital funding plan relies on drawing £3.010m from capital reserves for new additions, plus £0.6m from capital receipts not yet realised. Additionally, £2m of reserves is earmarked for the future Heritage Lottery match funding on Market Chambers. The document emphasises this reserve reliance as 'important to note'.
findings.matters: Significant reserve drawdown reduces financial flexibility for emergencies; assumes unrealised capital receipts, which if not achieved would require deeper reserve depletion
findings.figures: £3,010,000 from capital reserves for new 2026/27 schemes; £600,000 assumed from unfunded capital receipts; £2,000,000 reserves earmarked for Heritage match funding
findings.quote: It is important to note that the Council funding of the 2026/27 capital programme is based on using council reserves and potential capital receipts. There will be a continued emphasis relating to the realisation of additional capital receipts during the year. The programme assumes £3.010m of expenditure will be funded from capital reserves, and £0.6m from unfunded receipts.

findings.paper_title: b) Capital Programme 2026/27 - 2028/29
findings.headline: Levelling Up Programme costs of £6.25m are forecast figures, not tendered quotes, and are explicitly 'subject to change'
findings.detail: The Council's £6.251m allocation for Market Hall, Burton Chambers and associated improvements is based on forecast costs rephased from the prior year. The document explicitly states these are 'not tendered figures' and acknowledges they remain 'subject to change', with revisions to be reported during the year.
findings.matters: Material cost overruns on untendered figures could force scope cuts, budget reallocation or additional reserve drawdown mid-year
findings.figures: £6,251,000 total (Market Hall £2.665m, Burton Chambers £2.727m, Fire Compliance £322k, Solar Panels £500k)
findings.quote: The capital budgets for the Levelling Up Programme are based on the latest forecast of costs however as these are not tendered figures, they are still subject to change and should there be any changes to the current forecast, these will be reported during the year.

findings.paper_title: b) Capital Programme 2026/27 - 2028/29
findings.headline: Market Chambers building repair costs are still being determined by survey; final bill is unknown
findings.detail: The Council purchased Market Chambers in Summer 2025 as part of the Levelling Up programme. Survey work has been completed and reports will arrive 'in the coming weeks', but roof, windows and façade repair costs remain unquantified. A Phase 1 allocation of £600,000 has been made to prevent deterioration pending the full survey results. Future Heritage Lottery delivery-stage works will require £2m match funding from reserves.
findings.matters: A recently acquired major asset's true repair liability is still unknown; Phase 1 could be exceeded, forcing contingency or further reserve drawdown
findings.figures: £600,000 Phase 1 works; future roof/windows/façade costs TBD; £2,000,000 earmarked for Heritage Lottery match funding
findings.quote: Since the final part of the purchase completed in Summer 2025, survey work has taken place, and reports will be available in the coming weeks. This will allow the Council to fully understand the costs of repair works to the roof, windows, and façade. Some work may be required in this financial year to ensure the building condition does not deteriorate further.

findings.paper_title: a) General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27
findings.headline: Business Rates forecasting is highly imprecise and volatile, subject to variations of hundreds of thousands of pounds
findings.detail: After reforms in 2013/14, councils now retain a portion of business rates but carry the collection risk. Debt collection rates, appeals, new retail/hospitality multipliers, and business closures create uncertainty that the council describes as high imprecision.
findings.matters: Business Rates are now 23% of Hyndburn's funding base. The council may need to draw on reserves mid-year if forecasts prove too optimistic, or has discretion to use surpluses if actual collections exceed budget.
findings.figures: Estimated Business Rates £3.955m in 2026/27 including £0.422m forecast surplus from prior year; described as subject to 'hundreds of thousands of pounds' variation
findings.quote: the imprecision in these estimates is regarded as high and could be subject to variations of hundreds of thousands of pounds. The volatility around these forecasts have increased due to the impact recent national and global issues have had on the Business Community.

findings.paper_title: a) General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27
findings.headline: Housing Benefits costs for exempt accommodation have increased significantly with £0.4m now unrecovered
findings.detail: The council processes Housing Benefit claims on behalf of the DWP but cannot recover costs for claims in certain categories. A significant increase in 'exempt properties' claims is now budgeted at £0.4m and expected to continue rising.
findings.matters: A growing unrecovered cost with no clear solution suggests a structural problem. The council has established a working group but no fix is visible yet.
findings.figures: £0.4m in 2025/26; expected to increase each year across the MTFS period
findings.quote: The Council has seen a significant increase over 2025/26 in claims related to the 'exempt properties' category of which the Council is unable to recover. In line with the expected outturn for the current financial year, additional costs of £0.4m were included in the 2025/26 budget for dealing with this issue, this will be increased each year across the MTFS period.

findings.paper_title: a) General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27
findings.headline: Food Waste Collection service from April 2026 has no government funding for ongoing costs
findings.detail: A new statutory duty requires the council to provide separate food waste collections from April 2026. Capital costs are grant-funded by DEFRA, but MHCLG has confirmed no new burdens funding for the recurring revenue cost.
findings.matters: This is a mandated service with a £0.3m annual cost borne entirely by the council. It represents a permanent reduction in discretionary spending power.
findings.figures: £0.300m annual revenue pressure from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: From April 2026 the Council is required to introduce a food waste collection service for residents... MHCLG has confirmed through the Finance Settlement that no new burdens funding will be made available. This results in an additional revenue pressure of £0.300m from 2026/27 onwards.

findings.paper_title: a) General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27
findings.headline: Hyndburn Leisure Trust requires an ongoing council subsidy of around £0.5m per year
findings.detail: The outsourced leisure service is not breaking even; increases in utility costs, minimum wage, and National Insurance have created a recurring deficit that the council must fund.
findings.matters: A material ongoing subsidy indicates a service unable to self-sustain. If leisure facility usage declines or costs spike further, the pressure on the council budget increases.
findings.figures: £0.5m annual support expected; included in 2026/27 budget
findings.quote: The Council's leisure services are outsourced and run by Hyndburn Leisure Trust. Increases over recent years in utility costs, minimum wage and more recently National Insurance, have all significantly impacted the Trusts ability to maintain a breakeven position. The Trust are in the process of setting their budget for 2026/27, but it is expected that they will require financial support from the Council of around £0.5m.

findings.paper_title: a) General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27
findings.headline: Usable reserves are forecast to fall from £17.3m to £7.5m in a single year
findings.detail: The sharp decline is driven by capital spending and planned commitments. By March 2027, the council will have drawn down reserves by 57% in one year, leaving less headroom for future shocks.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion of this scale limits the council's ability to handle unexpected pressures, particularly given the upcoming funding cuts and business rates volatility.
findings.figures: £17.346m (31 March 2026) reducing to £7.507m (31 March 2027); drawdown of £9.839m
findings.quote: The table below shows the forecast position for the Councils usable reserves as at 31st March 2026 at £17.346m, with this further reducing to £7.507m by 31st March 2027.

findings.paper_title: a) General Fund Revenue Budget 2026/27
findings.headline: Hyndburn is set to lose 5% of funding by 2028/29 as a result of the Fair Funding Review
findings.detail: The council was identified as one of the hardest hit by government funding reforms. The loss is phased over three years, creating a structural deficit that will require either savings or reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: A 5% funding loss on a £17.6m budget is material. A lender needs to understand the council's plan to absorb this without deteriorating reserves or cutting services.
findings.figures: 5% loss by 2028/29; current funding £17,607,700
findings.quote: Hyndburn Council was highlighted early on in the consultation process as being one of hardest hit by the changes and this was confirmed in the December Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement. As such Hyndburn is set to lose 5% of funding by 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/2027 - 2028/2029
findings.headline: The council retains only 25% of its business rates income; central redistribution is rising
findings.detail: The council collects business rates but retains only 25% for local use after government (50%), county council and fire authority (10%) take their shares and the tariff system redistributes to other authorities. Hyndburn is a tariff authority—paying in rather than receiving. The business rates reset in 2026/27 introduces new vulnerability: councils falling below their baseline get safety-net protection at 100% in 2026/27, but only 97% in 2027/28 and 92.5% in 2028/29. Business rates volatility is now a revenue risk the council cannot fully control.
findings.matters: A lender would see that the council's exposure to business rate appeals, closures, and non-payment is rising at precisely the moment it needs more, not less, local revenue. The safety net withdrawal exposes the council to collection risk it did not face before.
findings.figures: Council retains 25% of business rates; safety net falls from 100% (2026/27) to 97% (2027/28) to 92.5% (2028/29); 2025/26 baseline £4.0m retained
findings.quote: As a result, Hyndburn ultimately retains only around 25% of business rates income for local use, with the remainder redistributed to Government or other local authorities... This safety net is only guaranteed for the 2026/27 financial year and will fall to 97% and 92.5% in 2027/28 and 2028/29 respectively.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/2027 - 2028/2029
findings.headline: Wage settlement assumptions of 2.5% are at risk; a 4% scenario (pessimistic model) would drive savings targets above 15%
findings.detail: The Standard Model assumes 2.5% annual pay awards, but the council acknowledges that wage settlements have risen sharply and unions are pressing for higher awards. The pessimistic scenario models 4% settlements, which would add £0.678m in costs over three years and push the 2028/29 savings requirement to 15.62%. This would "add substantially to the pressure to reduce the size of the workforce." Staff costs are the largest budget line at just under £14m.
findings.matters: A lender would see that if national pay negotiations deliver higher settlements, the council's already-tight savings plan collapses and forced redundancies become likely, triggering reputational risk, potential legal challenge, and further erosion of service quality.
findings.figures: Staff costs £14m; standard model assumes 2.5% pay award; pessimistic model assumes 4%; adds £0.678m over MTFS period
findings.quote: The Standard Model for 2026/2027 has assumed wage settlements of around 2.5%, and this is maintained across the MTFS period. The Pessimistic Model therefore outlines the impact on the Council's finances if Wage Settlements were at 4% for all years above the current inflation rate of 3.4%.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/2027 - 2028/2029
findings.headline: The capital programme depends on achieving significant asset sales; delayed or missed disposals would force cuts or borrowing
findings.detail: The council has maintained a policy of not borrowing to finance capital expenditure. However, Section 11.8 warns: "Current predictions indicate the Council has sufficient funds to finance its capital expenditure plans over the next 3 years. This is however reliant on the achievement of significant capital receipts over the period." If asset sales are delayed or fall through, the council would need to curtail capital spending or breach its no-borrowing commitment, further pressuring the revenue budget.
findings.matters: A lender would need to know whether the council is hedging against sale delays, what assets are pledged, and what contingency exists if the housing market or commercial property sales weaken.
findings.figures: £56.509m approved capital programme 2025/26; reliance on capital receipts for funding beyond 2026/27
findings.quote: Current predictions indicate the Council has sufficient funds to finance its capital expenditure plans over the next 3 years. This is however reliant on the achievement of significant capital receipts over the period and continuing to only fund the Council's highest priority projects. If the sale income from anticipated disposals is delayed or sales in the pipeline do not mature, decisions around curtailing capital expenditure or using some stop gap funding including short term borrowing may be necessary.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/2027 - 2028/2029
findings.headline: The council faces unfunded budget gaps of £2.2m and £2.8m in 2027/28 and 2028/29, requiring savings of 12–15% of the budget each year
findings.detail: The Standard Model (most likely scenario) shows the council can balance 2026/27 with £0.5m savings, but faces cumulative gaps of £5.1m over three years. These require service reductions of 12.31% in 2027/28 and 15.35% in 2028/29. The council acknowledges that "the cumulative impact of delivering savings over a long period of time makes this more difficult each year." In the pessimistic scenario, savings of 13.72% and 15.62% are required.
findings.matters: A lender would assess delivery risk: the council has not articulated how to find these savings without cutting services materially or triggering a Section 114 notice (illegal budget), and such large year-on-year cuts erode financial resilience and service quality.
findings.figures: Cumulative funding gap £5.065m; 2027/28 gap £2.222m (12.31%); 2028/29 gap £2.843m (15.35%); pessimistic model £6.378m cumulative
findings.quote: The standard model assumes a budget gap of 12.31% of the expenditure budget in 2027/28 and 15.35% 2028/29

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/2027 - 2028/2029
findings.headline: The council is losing 5% of its funding by 2028/29 despite being the 16th most deprived borough in England
findings.detail: Under the Fair Funding Review 2.0, Hyndburn was identified as one of the authorities furthest from its target funding level and will lose £6.35m in government grant over the MTFS period. The council is among the lowest funded in the country, yet the government's stated aim to strengthen the link between funding and deprivation has not protected it. District councils have been "the hardest hit group following the fair funding reforms."
findings.matters: A lender would need to know that the council's financial pressure is structural and not merely cyclical—driven by government policy allocation rather than local mismanagement—and that no economic recovery will reverse it within this period.
findings.figures: £6.35m reduction in government funding across the MTFS period; loss of 5% by 2028/29; Hyndburn ranked 16th most deprived (2025 IMD)
findings.quote: Hyndburn was identified early on as being one of the authorities furthest from the target funding level, losing 5% of its funding by 2028/29

findings.paper_title: PIs, Capital, TM and Investment Strategies 2026/27-2028/28 - Covering Report and Appendices 1-4
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting increases total debt reporting by £4m+, affecting debt ratios
findings.detail: Implementation of IFRS 16 in April 2024 required recognition of operating lease obligations (primarily vehicles) as balance sheet liabilities. Total debt is now £13.683m (2025/26) compared to market loans of only £9.595m, with the £4.088m difference being lease liabilities. This is a technical accounting change that does not reflect new borrowing but materially changes how external observers assess the council's debt position.
findings.matters: Lenders and rating agencies assess councils using debt metrics and leverage ratios. The lease accounting change means the council's apparent debt burden is substantially higher than in previous years, which could affect credit ratings or borrowing terms if not understood.
findings.figures: Market Loans £9,595k (unchanged) + Other Long-Term Liabilities £4,088k (lease obligations) = Total Debt £13,683k (2025/26)
findings.quote: This change relates to assets leased by the Council on operating leases (leases where the risks and rewards of ownership do not substantially transfer to the lessee).

findings.paper_title: PIs, Capital, TM and Investment Strategies 2026/27-2028/28 - Covering Report and Appendices 1-4
findings.headline: Cash reserves forecast to fall sharply from £38.8m to £10m in single year
findings.detail: Cash balances are forecast to decline from £38.768m in 2025/26 to £10m in 2026/27 and remain at that level. The document explicitly attributes high current cash to grants received in advance of capital spend, meaning the reserves are not freely available and reflect grant timing rather than underlying financial strength.
findings.matters: The apparent reserve cushion is temporary and grant-dependent. The sharp decline in 2026/27 creates a specific window where the council's liquidity position shifts materially, requiring careful cash forecasting and potentially constraining flexibility if capital spend timing slips.
findings.quote: Borrowing levels are above the liability benchmark due to high cash balances as a result of grants received in advance of capital spend, as well as the Council holding healthy levels of reserves.

findings.paper_title: PIs, Capital, TM and Investment Strategies 2026/27-2028/28 - Covering Report and Appendices 1-4
findings.headline: Financing costs ratio jumps to 27.5% in 2025/26 due to shift to vehicle leasing model
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is forecast to increase from 6.3% in 2024/25 to 27.5% in 2025/26, then decline to 23.3% (2026/27) and 18.9% (2027/28) as the leasing arrangements mature. This represents a material and temporary increase in the revenue budget allocated to debt servicing, driven by the council's decision to move its vehicle fleet to leasing rather than ownership.
findings.matters: A 27.5% financing cost ratio consumes significant revenue budget. While temporary, this constrains funds available for service delivery during that period and indicates a deliberate restructuring of how the council funds capital assets.
findings.quote: The ratio is forecast to increase from 25/26 as the Council moves to a leasing model for its vehicles.

findings.paper_title: Combined Audit Strategy and Completion Report for backstopped audits HBC Client
findings.headline: Prior significant weakness in financial reporting has been resolved
findings.detail: A 2020/21 audit identified a significant weakness: the council was producing draft accounts late and those accounts contained material errors. The council has now recruited additional finance staff to strengthen capacity and implemented a detailed action plan to speed up the accounts production process. The 2024/25 accounts were successfully published in June 2025, meeting the statutory deadline.
findings.matters: Financial reporting timeliness and accuracy are critical indicators of council management. Resolution of a prior capacity problem suggests the council has addressed an underlying control weakness.
findings.figures: Accounts published June 2025 (deadline met); additional staff recruited to finance team
findings.quote: During 2023/24 and 2024/25, the Council made good progress in addressing this weakness and implemented the recommendations made in previous years. Including continued implementation of the detailed action plan for reducing time scale for Statement of Accounts preparation process and recruitment of additional staff to strengthen the finance team and improve capacity.

findings.paper_title: Combined Audit Strategy and Completion Report for backstopped audits HBC Client
findings.headline: No substantive testing performed on any financial statement balances or transactions this year
findings.detail: Because of the backstop date constraint, auditors did not perform substantive testing procedures on the financial statement numbers. This means the balances and transactions reported in the accounts have not been independently verified by audit.
findings.matters: Without substantive testing, there is no independent verification that the numbers in the accounts are accurate, increasing the risk of undetected material misstatements.
findings.figures: Overall materiality set at £1.02m; performance materiality £0.61m
findings.quote: Due to the backstop, we have not undertaken substantive testing procedures on any balances or transactions reported in the accounts. Consequently, there are no misstatements to report.

findings.paper_title: Combined Audit Strategy and Completion Report for backstopped audits HBC Client
findings.headline: Fourth consecutive year the council has not received a clean audit opinion
findings.detail: Auditors have issued disclaimed opinions on the financial statements for 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25, meaning they express no opinion and provide no assurance. This is because insufficient audit procedures could be completed before each year's statutory backstop date of 27 February, which requires the council to publish its accounts whether or not the audit is complete.
findings.matters: A lender needs audit assurance over a council's financial statements to understand its true financial position. A four-year run of disclaimed opinions indicates unresolved audit issues and unverified financial statements.
findings.figures: Four consecutive years of disclaimers (2021/22 to 2024/25); backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: We issued a disclaimed opinion on your financial statements for 2021/22, 2022/23 and the 2023/24 financial years. This meant we did not express an opinion on those financial statements, and as such we do not have assurance over the opening balances in the 2024/25 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Prudiential Indicators Monitoring and Treasury Management Strategy Update - Q2 2025-26
findings.headline: £4.12m LOBO debt (43% of total borrowing) has 6-monthly lender call options, creating significant refinancing risk
findings.detail: Borrowings of £4.12m are structured as LOBO (Lender Option Borrower Option) agreements where lenders can call the debt every 6 months and demand refinancing at prevailing rates. This is classified as 'due within 12 months' in the maturity profile, creating regular refinancing pressure. If lenders exercise call options during a rising rate environment or tighter credit conditions, the council must refinance at potentially much higher cost.
findings.matters: LOBO debt creates chronic refinancing risk and rate volatility; the council has no protection against being forced to refinance nearly half its external debt at unfavourable rates
findings.figures: £4.12m LOBO borrowing; 43% of total external borrowing (£9.525m); call periods every 6 months
findings.quote: Borrowings of £4.12M are subject to LOBO (Lender Option Borrower Option) agreements. As they have call periods at 6 monthly intervals they are classed as borrowing under 12 months.

findings.paper_title: Prudiential Indicators Monitoring and Treasury Management Strategy Update - Q2 2025-26
findings.headline: Council plans to draw down useable reserves to fund revenue budget throughout the Medium-Term Financial Strategy period
findings.detail: The Liability Benchmark was revised to reflect increased drawdown of useable reserves to support the revenue budget over the MTFS period. Using reserves to fund day-to-day operations rather than addressing the structural deficit signals the council cannot balance its revenue budget from income and spending alone and is relying on one-off resources.
findings.matters: Planned reserve depletion is an unsustainable funding strategy and signals structural revenue deficits; lenders view this as a critical red flag indicating potential future financial distress
findings.figures: No amount specified; applies across full MTFS period
findings.quote: increased draw down of useable reserves anticipated to support the revenue budget over the MTFS period

findings.paper_title: Prudiential Indicators Monitoring and Treasury Management Strategy Update - Q2 2025-26
findings.headline: Finance lease liabilities more than doubled from £1.967m to £4.088m, driven by vehicle purchases, with interest costs massively exceeding budget
findings.detail: Other Long-Term Liabilities increased by £2.121m (108% increase) between the original estimate and Q2 forecast. More significantly, interest payable on finance leases is now forecast at £253k against a budget of only £41k—a £212k overspend. This indicates either unexpected vehicle purchase decisions or grossly inadequate original budgeting for an ongoing lease programme.
findings.matters: Unexpected lease liabilities and their interest costs reduce financial flexibility and indicate either poor capital planning or material unbudgeted commitments; lenders assess these as indicators of management control
findings.figures: Finance lease liabilities increase £2.121m (from £1.967m to £4.088m); interest payable forecast £253k vs budget £41k (overspend £212k)
findings.quote: An increase in finance leases relating to vehicle purchases has increased the liability and Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) totals.

findings.paper_title: Prudiential Indicators Monitoring and Treasury Management Strategy Update - Q2 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's gross debt exceeds Capital Financing Requirement by £2.372m, placing it in an over-borrowed position
findings.detail: The council is technically over-borrowed, with gross external debt of £13.683m against a CFR of £11.311m. The council attributes this to historic loans with maturity repayment structures, IFRS 16 lease accounting (particularly vehicles and equipment), and timing differences in capital expenditure. The council states no new external borrowing has occurred and it is not borrowing to support revenue spending, but the position requires monitoring as it indicates existing debt structures are not declining in line with the CFR.
findings.matters: Over-borrowing creates refinancing risk and is typically a sign of structural debt management challenges; lenders view this as a potential constraint on future borrowing capacity
findings.figures: Gross external debt £13.683m; CFR £11.311m; over-borrowing position £2.372m
findings.quote: the Council's gross debt is forecast to exceed the CFR by £2.372m, placing us in an over-borrowed position

news_drafts.headline: The council is planning to draw down useable reserves over the MTFS period to support the revenue budget
news_drafts.lead: Reserve drawdown to fund revenue is a sign of structural deficit; finite reserves depleting annually will eventually create a financial cliff unless underlying spending or income patterns change, creating risk for creditors.

news_drafts.lead: A rising financing ratio reduces budgetary flexibility for service delivery and indicates tightening affordability; it is a key metric for lenders assessing whether the council can service debt while maintaining service levels.
news_drafts.paper_title: PIs Monitoring and TM strategy Q1 2026/27 - Main Report

news_drafts.headline: Capital expenditure forecast has fallen to £18.823m from £44.265m budgeted in February—a 57% reduction in the first quarter
news_drafts.lead: Significant capital slippage can signal project delivery challenges, procurement delays, or inability to execute planned investment; it affects the CFR and medium-term financial sustainability.
